claims.quote: you can give the players a short summary instead

verdicts.trueWording: visualize him as an animal, and picture that animal as you describe
verdicts.note: Raw page (dmdavid.com tag archive carries the full 30 Jan 2024 post). Under heading 'DDA2 Legions of Thyatis (1990) by John Nephew' / 'Characterizing NPCs': 'One quick way to characterize an NPC is to visualize him as an animal, and picture that animal as you describe and play him.' Quote exact; adventure, year and author all match.

verdicts.trueWording: When you decide things aren't important, give the players a short summary instead
verdicts.note: Raw page, section 'The Hidden Halls of Hazacor (2018) by Scott Fitzgerald Gray' / 'Summarize the boring parts': 'When you decide things aren't important, you can give the players a short summary instead. Traveling is often best summarized.' Quote exact; the page also says the adventure 'gives first-time DMs an adventure stocked with guidance', supporting 'new DMs'.

verdicts.trueWording: The adventures even include scripted text for the DM to read to new players
verdicts.note: Raw page, section 'Eye of the Wyvern (1999) by Jeff Grubb': 'Eye of the Wyvern and its twin adventure Wrath of the Minotaur both teach the game... The adventures even include scripted text for the DM to read to new players who apparently have no idea what activity awaits them.' Quote exact; post dated January 30, 2024 by David Hartlage. Minor: the page dates only Eye of the Wyvern to 1999, calling Wrath of the Minotaur its 'twin adventure' without a year, so the plural '1999 modules' rests on the pairing.

verdicts.trueWording: Casual DMs could simply buy an adventure, read the boxed text
verdicts.note: Raw page, post of February 14, 2023 by David Hartlage: 'Skill challenges satisfied three design goals... To make the DM's role undemanding. Casual DMs could simply buy an adventure, read the boxed text, and then run a sequence of skill challenges and combat encounters.' Skill challenges are the fourth-edition innovation the post is about, so 'fourth-edition design goal' holds.

verdicts.trueWording: the 1980 adventure module The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan marks its first appearance
verdicts.note: Raw page, byline 'December 18, 2023 Brian McKenzie': 'Called read-aloud or boxed text (because it is typically set outside from the other text in a box), the 1980 adventure module The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan marks its first appearance.' Quote exact; McKenzie cites Merric Blackman at note 31 for this.

verdicts.trueWording: Read-aloud text is analogous to 'at rise' descriptions
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'D&D adventure writers employ descriptive text in the same way as playwrights use “at rise” descriptions.' and 'Read-aloud text is analogous to “at rise” descriptions.' The page defines 'at rise' as text describing the stage when the curtain rises and treats it as a genre convention, supporting 'genre analogue'.

verdicts.trueWording: Hints of what may be done are given in this text
verdicts.note: Raw page quotes the module: 'Hints of what may be done are given in this text and the DM should only provide vague information if questioned.' Introduced as 'The authors of The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan instruct DMs...They explain its purpose'; endnote 34 is Johnson and Leason, The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan (TSR, 1980), 2 - matching the claim's note and attribution.

verdicts.trueWording: Read-aloud text is, in short, an aid to players
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'Read-aloud text is, in short, an aid to players. It offers clues and the frames narrative boundaries.' Quote exact, including the source's own typo 'the frames'.

verdicts.trueWording: Cover offers one of the few - perhaps the only - academic discussions
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'Cover offers one of the few—perhaps the only—academic discussions of read-aloud text in TTRPG adventures.' Quote exact with em dashes; the endnote identifies Cover as Jennifer Grouling Cover, The Creation of Narrative in Tabletop Role-Playing Games (McFarland, 2014).

verdicts.trueWording: if our D&D game is a Broadway show, our read-aloud text is part of our script
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'The prolific D&D author Michael Shea...makes an explicit connection between read-aloud text and drama: “if our D&D game is a Broadway show, our read-aloud text is part of our script.”' Endnote 35 is Shea, 'Writing Awesome Read-Aloud Text', Sly Flourish, 2010 - matching the claim's note.

Raw page: 'A Twitter poll by D&D's current lead rules designer Jeremy Crawford saw 2,248 replies to the question “How much boxed text (aka read-aloud text) do you like in an adventure you run?” The results were 59.5% desired “occasional boxed text,” 34.4% “lots of boxed text,” and only 6% of respondents did not want any boxed text.' Every figure and the role match; endnote 38 is the Crawford tweet (17 Nov 2016).

verdicts.trueWording: It's as much a part of D&D's history and brand as saving throws
verdicts.note: Raw page (dndbeyond.com, 'by Shawn Merwin', Nov 6, 2019), opening paragraph: 'It's as much a part of D&D's history and brand as saving throws, hit points, and armor class.' Quote exact (curly apostrophe in D&D's); subject is boxed text, 'also sometimes referred to as read-aloud text'.

verdicts.trueWording: the very act of having to write it, to think harder about their encounters
verdicts.note: Raw page, third paragraph: 'It can also force adventure designers, by the very act of having to write it, to think harder about their encounters.' Quote exact. Merwin's wording is the modal 'can also force' inside a 'when it's good' clause, where the claim states it flatly; the proposition itself is his.

verdicts.trueWording: relies on five elements to embed the critical ideas
verdicts.note: Raw PDF (19pp, text extracted), p. 145: 'The design of the adventure relies on five elements to embed the critical ideas: plot (including encounters), read-aloud text, player handouts, instructions to the Dungeon Master (DM), and NPC dialogue.' Quote exact; authors McKenzie, Zawilski and Beirne, IJRP Issue 17, article titled a 'Case Study of a Commercial Dungeons & Dragons Adventure'. The source's word is 'elements', not 'textual elements', and the fifth is plot.

verdicts.trueWording: many early examples lack prose and narrative in favor of rules
verdicts.note: Raw page, byline 'December 18, 2022 Stefan Huddleston', section 'Sidebar: A Note on Primary Sources': 'Presumably, TTRPG rule books have been ignored for their primary source value because many early examples lack prose and narrative in favor of rules.' Quote exact; the subject is TTRPG rule books, matching 'early tabletop rulebooks'.
